name: Stablecoin Stress Testing
title: Stablecoin Stress Testing
answer: Stablecoin stress testing is the practice of modelling how a token pegged to a fiat currency behaves when redemption pressure, market dislocation or reserve doubts hit at once. It covers fiat backed coins, crypto collateralised coins and algorithmic designs, and it looks at the peg, the reserve, the redemption queue and the secondary market together. The work sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, where a broken peg can cascade through lending pools and exchanges within hours.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Stablecoin stress testing is the practice of modelling how a token pegged to a fiat currency behaves when redemption pressure, market dislocation or reserve doubts hit at once. It covers fiat backed coins, crypto collateralised coins and algorithmic designs, and it looks at the peg, the reserve, the redemption queue and the secondary market together. The work sits inside crypto markets and decentralised finance, where a broken peg can cascade through lending pools and exchanges within hours.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The inputs are on chain and off chain at the same time. On chain data covers mint and burn events, pool balances, collateral ratios and liquidation activity, while off chain data covers reserve attestations, bank and treasury holdings, and exchange order books. Teams typically run simulations against historical stress windows and live feeds, using node access, indexers and market data vendors, and they keep a separate model for each issuer because reserve structures differ.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A test starts by defining a shock, such as a large redemption, a reserve write down, a depeg in collateral or a loss of a key banking partner. The model then traces who can exit first, how fast the peg recovers or fails, and which protocols absorb the loss. Common techniques include agent based simulation, historical replay, liquidity gap analysis and scenario grids, with results expressed as peg deviation, redemption coverage and contagion paths rather than a single pass or fail number.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Stress results feed into risk limits, disclosure and supervisory dialogue, and they are only as good as the reserve data behind them. Attestations, audit scope, redemption terms and the legal claim on reserves all shape what a test can honestly claim, and regulators in several jurisdictions now expect issuers to show how they would handle a run. Provenance matters here, so a test should record its data sources, assumptions and version history, and it should be clear about what is verified on chain and what is taken on trust.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent, more standardised and more automated testing, with reserve data pulled closer to real time and scenarios shared across firms. Tokenised treasury products, multi chain issuance and cross border redemption add new failure modes that current models handle poorly. Expect stress testing to become a routine part of issuance, listing and lending decisions rather than a periodic exercise, and expect the assumptions behind each test to be published alongside the result.
